newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends firmer on U.S. data, Seguin's comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firmer on U.S. data, Seguin's comments.

text.p: *Dlr/mark ends slightly below 1.7074 U.S. high, supported by France's Seguin who said he wants a broad-based, looser euro. *Dlr firmed after May consumer conf index jumps to 127.1, 28-yr high. Apr existing home sales -2.4 percent slowed gain. *Dlr/yen firm on sidelines. *Bank of Canada buys Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars at around C$1.3830, traders said.

The dollar rose on Tuesday as investors flocked to the safe haven of greenbacks amid worries about the implication of France's parliamentary election for Europe's proposed monetary union, traders said.
A strong left-wing showing in France's first round of elections on Sunday sparked concern that strict European economic and monetary union (EMU) entry rules could be bent to fit political wishes.
The dollar rose to 1.7045/55 marks by the close from 1.6975/85 at the open and 116.64/69 yen from 116.35/45.
Fueling the EMU controversy was an announcement on Monday by France's unpopular conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe that he will resign.

One of his potential successors, French National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, sent the dollar to session highs on Tuesday by saying he favors looser fiscal criteria and a larger pool of entrants in the first wave of EMU.
Seguin's remarks, to be published on Wednesday in the weekly magazine L'Express, were reported by wire services at the U.S. midday.

"Even if there is an ultimate center-right victory, you're still looking at a weaker, laxer EMU. It will be difficult to pass any fiscal austerity measures with a large protest vote," said Andrew Hodge, a financial strategist at Bank Brussels Lambert in New York.

France's opposition socialist party, which looks set to wrest power from the ruling right-wing coalition in the second round of elections on June 1, supports EMU but places heavy emphasis on growth and jobs. It also wants Italy and Spain to join EMU in the first wave of membership in 1999.
Also bolstering the U.S. unit was data showing a surge in U.S. consumer optimism in May.
On Tuesday, the Conference Board said its index of consumer confidence surged to 127.1 -- its highest level in 28 years.
The consumer sentiment number followed a revised 118.5 in April and came against forecasts of 118.1 for the May index.

"Consumer confidence at a 28-year high seemed to revive speculation of U.S. interest rate hikes. So you've got that and the French elections giving some boost to the dollar," said Mike Malpede, senior analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
But the greenback's rise was temporarily slowed by simultaneous data showing a 2.4 percent decline in April existing home sales, traders said.
Home sales, fell to a 4.06 million unit annual rate from a revised 4.16 million unit pace in March. Forecasts averaged 4.09 million units, annualized.

The dollar also gained against the Swiss franc, despite its traditional status as a safe haven in times of EMU uncertainty, after senior officials at Switzerland's central bank said they were unhappy with the franc's recent strength.

Swiss National Bank president Hans Meyer said on Tuesday he was not content with the recent strengthening of the franc. This was echoed by SNB vice chairman Jean-Pierre Roth who also said the central bank was not ruling out lower money market interest rates.

The dollar rose to 1.4203/13 Swiss francs from 1.4150/60 and the British pound inched lower to $1.6305/15 from $1.6318/28. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3842/47 from C$1.3766/71 despite the Bank of Canada buying Canadian dollars for U.S. dollars at roughly C$1.3830 per dollar, traders said.
The Australian dollar fell to $0.7645/50 from $0.7654/59.
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
